title: TypeScript versus JavaScript and C#
hook: TypeScript is JavaScript with a compile-time type checker layered on top. Unlike C#, whose types survive into Intermediate Language (IL) and are enforced by the Common Language Runtime (CLR), TypeScript types disappear before any engine runs your code.

blocks.text: JavaScript is the language browsers and Node.js execute. TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript: you write .ts files, the TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks types, then emits plain .js that runs anywhere JavaScript runs. C# is a different family entirely — it compiles to IL for the CLR, keeps type metadata in assemblies, and enforces types at run time. TypeScript gives you static analysis without changing the JavaScript runtime model.

entries.plainDefinition: The official tool that type-checks TypeScript and emits JavaScript.
entries.example: npx tsc --noEmit only checks types without writing .js files.

entries.plainDefinition: Valid JavaScript is valid TypeScript; TypeScript adds optional syntax like type annotations.
entries.example: const x = 1; works in both .js and .ts files.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET host that loads assemblies and enforces run-time types — not the same as V8 or another JavaScript engine.
entries.example: A .NET Lambda runs on the CLR; a Node Lambda runs on V8.

blocks.text: Treating TypeScript like "C# for the browser" leads to wrong assumptions about deployment, debugging, and safety. A Redis client in C# holds a real typed object the CLR understands. A TypeScript interface describes shape only until JavaScript runs — JSON.parse returns a plain object with no interface tag. When you ship a Node service next to a .NET worker, both may consume the same Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) JSON, but only C# preserves nominal types through deserialization into assembly-defined classes.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: JavaScript is what runs. TypeScript checks then erases. C# compiles to IL with real types the CLR enforces. Three different layers — do not collapse them.

items.title: JavaScript
items.body: Source or bundled .js executed by V8, SpiderMonkey, or another engine. Types are dynamic at run time (typeof, instanceof).

items.title: TypeScript
items.body: Optional static checking at build time. Output is JavaScript — engines never see your interfaces or generics.

items.title: C#
items.body: Roslyn compiles to IL + metadata. The CLR JIT-compiles to machine code and enforces types when your app runs.

diagram.title: TypeScript vs JavaScript vs C# hosts

  end

sections.heading: Code walkthrough: same idea, different runtimes

snippet.label: TypeScript adds checking, emits JavaScript
snippet.explanation: TypeScript catches typos like order.odrId at compile time. After emit, only JavaScript runs — the interface never existed at run time. C# would deserialize into a real OrderCreated class in the assembly.

snippet.label: What the engine actually runs
snippet.explanation: Emitted JavaScript is what Node or the browser executes. Without a separate validator (Zod, manual checks), wrong shapes fail at run time with undefined or TypeError.

snippet.label: C# contrast — types survive compile (shown in TS comments)
snippet.explanation: C# types survive compilation. Invalid casts throw InvalidCastException at run time. TypeScript structural types erase — the engine only sees plain objects.

snippet.label: Valid JS is valid TS (gradual start)
snippet.explanation: TypeScript's superset design lets teams migrate file by file. C# requires explicit types from the start (with rare var inference). This is why brownfield JavaScript adoption of TypeScript is common.

blocks.title: TypeScript vs JavaScript vs C# at a glance
rows: Requires JS interop or separate service

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Saying TypeScript and C# are "both statically typed" without mentioning erasure vs CLR metadata. Assuming tsc output is safer at run time — it is not; only the check phase added safety. Deploying TypeScript source to production instead of compiled JavaScript (engines do not run .ts natively without a loader).

blocks.text: Production proof: TypeScript's value is developer velocity and refactor safety in the editor and CI — not run-time guarantees. Polyglot systems (Node BFF + .NET API) share JSON schema or OpenAPI, not types. C# DTOs and TS interfaces diverge unless you codegen from one source. TypeScript 5.x can run via tsx or ts-node for dev, but production Node still executes emitted JS or uses a bundler (esbuild, swc) that strips types without full tsc semantics.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming TypeScript runs in the browser natively without transpilation. Equating tsc to dotnet build. Saying TS interfaces exist at run time like C# classes. Ignoring that JSON.parse in TS is as unsafe at run time as in JS unless you validate.

interviewTakeaways: TypeScript is a compile-time layer on JavaScript; types erase before V8 or any engine runs your code.
C# types live in IL metadata and are enforced by the CLR — a fundamentally different contract than TS interfaces.
Polyglot teams need OpenAPI, JSON Schema, or codegen — never assume TS interfaces match C# DTOs.
60s: JS runs everywhere. TS checks then emits JS. C# compiles to IL with real types on the CLR. Same JSON event, different hosts and type systems. tsc is not dotnet build.
Follow-up: when would you add Zod or runtime validation on a TypeScript API boundary?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'TypeScript is statically typed like C#.' Strong: 'TS checks at compile time then erases; C# keeps types in IL for CLR enforcement.'
Assuming shipping .ts files to production works without a build step — engines execute JavaScript.
Strong answer: 'Three layers: JS runtime, TS checker, optional C# CLR worker. Contract is schema, not shared interfaces.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Every valid .js file can be renamed .ts. TypeScript adds optional annotations without changing the JavaScript execution model.
TypeScript interfaces erase on emit. C# compiles to IL with metadata the CLR enforces — compare when designing polyglot APIs.
